analytic.title: Schedulability Analysis for MultiCore Global Scheduling with Model Checking

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

textClass.keywords: Real-Time Systems ； Multicore Scheduling; Verification； Model Checking

div.p: With the development of multicore systems, multicore real time scheduling is becoming a hot topic in time-critical systems. Cache warm-up overheads introduced by task migration between two cores can result in missed deadlines for tight realtime schedules. In this paper, we present an exact method for multicore schedulability analysis under cache warm-up overheads. The result of the analysis is used to determine whether it's necessary to change the scheduling algorithm or the hardware architecture. Correct and schedulable properties of the model are formalized and verified. It is shown that our approach is less pessimistic than bound tests.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Due to thermal and power problems, single-processor designs encountered challenges. Multicore architectures, which contain several processors on a single chip, have been proposed. Multicore/multiprocessor scheduling draws lots of attention. It can be classified into as two categories, partitioned and global. In partitioned scheduling, once a task is assigned into a core, it will not be migrated into another one. Partitioning tasks into cores optimally is an NP-Hard problem. If new tasks arrive at a partitioned scheduling system, the entire system has to be re-distributed. To address these limitations, global scheduling has been proposed.

In multicore global scheduling, task migration among cores is pervasive. We focus on the multicore architecture shown in Figure 1, wherein all cores are symmetric. Each core has L1 and L2 cache individually. They share a chip-wide L3 cache. This architecture has been studied actively. When a task is migrated from a core where its cache (L1+L2) has the cache lines of the task (a warm cache for the task) into a core while the cache of the core doesn't own the cache lines of the task (a cold cache for the task), the worst-case execution time (WCET) of the task expands. It is because the task has to spend time in bringing cache lines from a shared L3 cache or the warm cache to the cold cache. The extra time is called cache warm-up overheads, which have an impact on real-time systems since any dilation in execution time of real-time tasks could lead to the failure of systems [1].

Schedulability analysis is to determine whether a given task set can meet its deadlines under a scheduling algorithm. In multicore or multiprocessor field, there are mainly two methods for schedulability analysis: bound tests and simulation. The first method is based on utilization or slack of tasks, which is safe but pessimistic since it rejects some schedulable tasksets. The second approach is unreliable since it only tests finite execution traces, not all the traces. Under cache warm-up overheads, there is not an exact method for schedulability analysis of multicore global scheduling. In this paper, we provide an exact approach for solving the problem without the flaws of bound tests and simulation. The approach is based on model checking, which can explore the entire system state space and check properties. The model checker UPPAAL [2] is used for verification since it can model not only a continuous time model but also a discrete time model. The scheduling system is formalized by timed automata [3]. The abstract model doesn't introduce any clock variables, so it can be moved to other non-timed model checkers (eg. NuSMV) or be modified for a continuous time model accepted by UPPAAL. Our method reduces the pessimism of bound tests. For simplification, we only consider the environment of two cores. In our model, preemption delay and communication delay between two cores are either negligible. The time spent on context switches is not concerned. The scheduling algorithm is work conserving, i.e., there are no idle cores when a ready task is waiting for execution.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Related work is discussed in Sect. II. We show a timed automata model in Sect. III. The related properties are verified in Sect. IV. Finally, we draw conclusions in Sect. V.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: Some research efforts focus on multiprocessor global real time scheduling. The Pfair class of global scheduling algorithms has been proposed [4][5][6]. These algorithms change the priority of a job in its execution. The drawback is to induce a job to switch context and migrate frequently. To solve this disadvantage, in some scheduling the priority of a task can change at job boundaries or all the jobs of a task have the same priority [7][8][9][10][11]. However, they don't concern the impact of cache for scheduling, which is important for multicore realtime scheduling. For solving task competition in a shared cache, [12] proposes cache space isolation techniques and presents schedulability bound tests. Due to task migration, [1,13] proposes a new micro architecture to reduce the cache warm-up overheads and give some policies for migration, which increase timing predictability in practice.

Schedulability analysis is an important problem in realtime scheduling systems. Bound tests is a classical method. A task τ i = (C i ,D i ,T i ) in a taskset is characterized by a WCET C i , a deadline D i , and a period or minimum interarrival time T i . The number of processors is m. [10] presents a utilization bound tests, where a taskset contains some periodic tasks while the relative deadline of each task equals its period. div.p: We will compare our approach to the bound tests in [10] and [11] in Sect. IV. Some researchers use model checking for schedulability test. [14,15] concerns single-processor scheduling environments. While some studies focus on multicore circumstances. [16] transforms a multicore schedulability test problem into the reachability checking problem of timed automata. Using a discrete time model checker NuSMV, [17] presents an approach for schedulability test of global multiprocessor scheduling with Fixed-Priority and EDF algorithms. However, their models don't consider the effect of task migration in real-time scheduling. Due to cold cache, task migration induces WCET dilation for a task. It brings significant challenges into schedualbility test, which is our focus in this paper.

div.head: III. TIMED AUTOMATA MODEL
div.p: In this section, under cache warm-up overheads we build a multicore global scheduling timed automata model for periodic tasks with preemptive RM algorithm. To reduce the state space of the model, we only consider scheduling in dual core environments. The model is based on conventional hardware warm-up architecture (Pull-based model [13]), where its cache (L1+L2) misses are resolved one at a time using a coherence protocol. Unless stated, a cache of a core means its L1 and L2 cache.

div.head: A. Definition
div.p: In a uniprocessor scenario, one can get the WCET of a task by static timing analysis when all the cache lines of the task are in the cache of the processor. The cache is warm for the task. However, in a multicore environment, task migration may result in a task runs on a core whose local cache does not own the task cache lines. Only if not all the cache lines of the task are in the cache, the cache is regarded as cold (for the task).
Two cases are shown as follows: 1) A task runs on a core (source) while its cache is warm.
2) The next release of the task is invoked on a core (target) where its cache is cold.

The WCET of a task in the first case is called BeforeWCET, which means WCET before migration. It is computed when enough resources are in the cache of the source core, which means any cache misses do not happen during the execution of the task. The WCET in the second case is named AfterWCET (WCET after migration). Each cache miss on the target core results in cache lines migration. AfterWCET = WUT+BeforeWCET, where WUT is all the time of reading cache lines from a shared L3 cache or the L1/L2 caches of the source core to the cache of the target core.

In the experimental model from [1], a real-time application comprises periodic tasks. For a task, its job is defined as an instance of its execution. Job 0 of a task is used to warm the local cache of a core, and then job 1 must run on the same core while its cache is warm. In our model, for simplicity the first instance of a task (job 1) must run on a core where its cache is warm, even though it may be preempted later. It can be understood since it is easy to know which core job 1 runs on. The system can make some warm-up initialization, which is the function of job 0. The experiment results from [1] show that WCET in cold cache (AfterWCET) is higher than WCET in warm cache (BeforeWCET) from less than a percent to 56.6 percent in given benchmarks. We will use the results in our model. For a task, the deadline of each job is equal and their execution time varies due to cache warm-up overheads.

div.head: B. Simplification
div.p: The most difficult part in our experiment is modeling the execution time of a job in multicore scheduling when cache warm-up overheads are considered. In modeling an abstract scheduling system, to determine when a job finishes, the WCET of the job should be given before the job runs.

A job is migrated often between two cores in its period. When it suffers from cache misses, the job reads cache lines from a shared L3 cache or the cache of the source core respectively under MESI and MOESI coherence protocols. The number of cache misses is not known before the job runs. The time spent in reading cache lines is hard to forecast. For estimating the WCET of a job exactly, the time should be involved in the execution time of the job.
For a task, there are two reasons for cache misses: the requested cache line in a cache is invalid the requested cache line is not in the cache

In dual-core global scheduling, a job can be migrated between two cores several times during its period. A cache line of the job may be in each cache of the two cores. Suppose that a cache line in a cache is L and the same cache line in the other cache is L'. Assuming L of a job is modified in a core, L' will become invalid according to MESI or MOESI. Once the job is migrated into the other core and L' is accessed, time will be consumed to read cache lines from L3 cache or the cache of the core. It is hard to formalize and predict the time induced by the first reason for cache misses. So we ignore the time.

In addition, the time spent in sending the coherence requests (e.g., an invalidation request) is not concerned. When a cache line becomes dirty, the cache will write it back or write it through to L3 cache. The time for writing into L3 cache is not considered.

In our model, the time spent in reading cache lines due to the second reason is called warm-up time (overhead). In the above case (in A. Definition), WUT is the warm-up time. When a job is migrated into a core owning a cold cache, it needs to warm up the cold cache. The warm-up time is piecemeal and the execution time of the job is difficult to calculate. For simplicity, the following theorem is introduced.

Theorem 1. In dual-core global preemptive scheduling considering cache warm-up overheads, if there is at most one core owning a cold cache for a task, the WCET of the task is not bigger than AfterWCET.

Proof. If two cores both have warm caches for a task, the WCET of the task is BeforeWCET(<=AfterWCET). If there is a core which has a cold cache, the task has to warm up the cache when it is migrated to the core. In preemptive scheduling, a task may be migrated between these two cores several times. The time that a task spends on a core while its cache is cold includes two parts: warm-up the cold cache and execute instructions. Figure 2 shows an execution path of a task between a cold cache and a warm cache in its period. Although the warm-up time is fragmented, the entire warm-up time in the cold cache is not bigger than WUT. Since WUT is the time of reading cache lines of a task from a warm cache to the cache which does not own any cache lines of the task. So the WCET of a task is not bigger than BeforeWCET+WUT.□ According to the theorem, a simplification is introduced. a) In a period of a task, once it is migrated into a core whose cache is cold, its execution time expands to AfterWCET.

For a task, a cold cache can become warm since the task often runs a core whose cache is cold. However it is difficult to determine when a cold cache becomes warm. Hence we introduce the following simplification. b) If a task always runs on a core having a cold cache during its period, the cold cache will become warm after it finishes. Otherwise, no cold caches can turn warm.

Multicore with large L2 cache has been an active research field [1]. To avoid tasks induce cache misses each other, each core has a L2 cache of a large size, which means all the required resources of some tasks are in the cache. This doesn't mean that L2 cache is big enough to contain cache lines of all the tasks. In addition, some tasks do not need to run on some cores.

div.head: C. Description
div.p: In modeling preemptive scheduling, continuous time formalism needs a stopwatch mechanism [18] or some approximation methods [14] to count a task's execution time. To model preemptive scheduling easily, we use discrete time formalism to build an abstract model, which means release time, preemptive time, period and WCET of a task are all integers.
Our model is composed of the automata Clock, Task and Scheduler. There are some Task automata concurrently running.

[16] models a discrete multiprocessor scheduling model and uses a clock variable (oc) to make system global time run step by step. When oc==TICK, it means that one digital clock has passed, where TICK is a constant. However, we don't use any clock variables. It makes our model move to other discrete model checkers easily (e.g., NuSMV). To make the system model run forward, the synchronization of automata is designed. At an integer time instant, some events must take place, for example task release, execution, finish and schedule. Schedule happens after all the other events at an instant. Schedule finish implies that the instant has passed.

Figure 3 shows a timed automaton Clock modeling global time interval. Initialization is in Begin(). In the location Interval, a task can release, run or finish. Once the transition Interval → C1 is taken, any tasks are not allowed to release or finish at this interval. Initially, a task releases during [0, P-1], where P is the period of the task. If a task has not released in [0, P-2], it must release at the instant P-1 and isOffsetChk is introduced. isOffsetChk is initialized to 1.The idea is to increase isOffsetChk by 1 at P-2 (Check()). At P-1, if the task releases, the automaton Task decreases isOffsetChk by 1 and isOffsetChk==1. Whether the transition is taken also depends on the other two variables: isRlsChk and isFlhChk. They are used to make a task release (not initially) and finish at a particular instant respectively. Their usages are similar to isOffsetChk. At a particular instant, if more than one task must release or finish, the Clock has to wait for all the tasks release or finish. If the three variables all equal 1, Interval → C1 takes place and schedstate is assigned to 1. schedstate is to avoid a task release initially after the transition. Once the transition is taken, no any tasks release or finish at this instant and the scheduler can be activated. Under warm-up overheads, determining the WCET of a job is important in the automaton Task. As shown in Figure 4, when a job is scheduled, if BeforeWCET[id]==AfterWCET [id] for the job, Ready → Run is taken. Otherwise, Ready → C1 is taken. For the clarity of presentation, we attach label numbers to several transitions in Figure 4.

C [id] is the WCET of a task in its period and is initialized to BeforeWCET [id]. isallcold [id] means whether a task always runs on a core id while its cache is cold. isallcold[id] is initialized to 0. All the caches are initialized to be cold. In the location C1, if C[id]==BeforeWCET[id], C1 → C2 is taken. Otherwise, C1 → C3 is taken. In C2, if a job runs on a core while its cache is warm (warmcache[twp[id]]==1), it goes through ③. Otherwise, it goes through ④. For the transition ④ , if job1 initially runs on a core, set the cache of the core warm. Otherwise (the job is not job 1 or job1 does not run on the core initially), C[id] is assigned to AfterWCET[id] since the simplification a). If the job is not job1, isallcold[twp [id]] is set as 1. Job1 does not always run on a core where its local cache is cold. These actions take place in UpdateWCET(id). In the location C3, if a job runs on a core where its cache is warm, the job does not always run on a core whose cache is cold (isallcold[1-twp[id]]=0) (⑤→⑥). In this situation, the cache of the core cannot become warm according to the simplification b). Otherwise, it goes through ⑦. For a task, whether a cold cache becomes warm depends on isallcold[twp [id]]==1 or 0 (C4 → C5). Figure 5 shows a timed automaton for a scheduler. When it receives a scheduling request from the channel sched, it enters into the location C1. If the ready queue is empty (rdynum==0), the scheduler does nothing (C1 → Init). Otherwise, it checks to see whether there are some idle cores. If yes (idlnum>0), the maximum priority task from the ready queue (id=MaxPrioTask()) is assigned into a core(C1 → C2). Otherwise, it checks to see whether a running task can be preempted (p=Prmpt(id)). If yes (p>=0), the task is preempted (C1 → C3 → C4). Otherwise, it returns to the location Init. More than one task may be scheduled, so the automaton may go through C2 or C3 and C4 more than one time.

div.head: IV. SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS
div.p: All properties have been verified by UPPAAL 4.10 running on Intel Core2 Duo (2.66GHz) CPU and 1.95GB RAM running Windows XP.

div.head: A. Correctness
div.p: Several properties need to be checked to guarantee the multicore scheduling model run correctly. They are listed as follows. Property 1: If the ready queue is not empty, the priority of each task in the ready queue is not higher than any running tasks. The property is formalized in the UPPAAL specification language as follows:

div.head: A[] rdynum>0 imply runmaxperiod <= rdyqminperiod
div.p: In preemptive RM algorithm, the priority of a task is based on its period. The smaller the period is, the higher is the priority. We compare the minimum priority of running tasks (runmaxperiod) and the maximum priority of tasks in the ready queue (rdyqminperiod). rdynum>0 means the ready queue is not empty. This property refers to the process of schedule and preemption in the model.

Property2: When a task always runs on cores which all have warm cache for the task, its WCET is BeforeWCET. Once a task runs a core which has a cold cache for the task, its WCET becomes AfterWCET. The property is formalized in the UPPAAL specification language as follows:

div.head: A[] isColdCache[id]==0 imply C[id] == BeforeWCET[id] A[] isColdCache[id]==1 imply C[id] == AfterWCET[id]
div.p: id is replaced by particular task ID for example 0,1,etc.

isColdCache [id] means whether a task id runs on a core while its cache is cold during its period. In our model, there are two cores. If a task is migrated from a warm cache to a cold cache (isColdCache[id]==1), its WCET is expanded into AfterWCET. If a task is migrated from a cold cache to a warm cache (isColdCache[id]==1), its WCET is still AfterWCET. Only if it always runs on a core while its cache is warm (isColdCache[id]==0), its WCET equals BeforeWCET. It consists with our simplification proposed in Sect.III. Our model is satisfied with the above properties.

div.head: B. Efficiency
div.p: The following table shows the parameters of our experiments. N is the number of tasks in each taskset. M is the number of cores. T represents the range of a task's period. BeforeWCET and AfterWCET is the WCET of a task running in a warm cache and a cold cache respectively. In our experiments, each taskset is generated by the above parameter value unless declared.
In our model, the schedulable property is formalized in the UPPAAL specification language as follows:

div.head: A[] error==0
div.p: The variable error is initialized as 0. From Figure 4, if a running task misses deadline (dcC[id]<C[id] && dcD[id]== D[id]) or a task in the ready queue misses deadline (dcD[id]==D[id]), the automaton Task will go into the location Error. The variable error is set as 1. So if this property is satisfied for a taskset in all the execution paths, it means the taskset is schedulable; otherwise the taskset is not schedulable.
Three schedulability tests are compared:

the bound test in There are 100 tasksets and the results are showed in Figure 6. Under cache warm-up overheads, AT(BW), BT(BW) and MC(BW) is unreliable since it underestimates the WCET of a task in a period. There are 10, 47, 82 and 86 schedulable tasksets with AT(AW), BT(AW), MC(AW) and MC(both) respectively. It is shown that MC(AW) provides less pessimistic results than both AT(AW) and BT(AW), which rejects some schedulable tasksets since it is sufficient but not necessary. Further, MC(both) is less pessimistic than MC(AW), since the WCET of a task is BW if the task runs on a core containing the warm cache, less than AW. Under cache warm-up overheads, we get another reason for the pessimism of bound tests: the WCET of a task is fixed and must be set as AW for reliable.

To illustrate the efficiency of MC(Both) further, we assume that AfterWCET of each task is ⎣ ⎦ BeforeWCET 56 . 1 MC(AW) is 87.5% higher than BT(AW), which shows that model checking is effective for determining schedulable tasksets.The number in MC(Both) is 43.3% higher than MC(AW). So it is important to model the WCET of tasks under warm cache and cold cache.

div.head: V. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: In multicore real time scheduling, task migration among multiple cores brings new challenges. Cache warm-up overheads make task execution time expand. So it is necessary to evaluate scheduling algorithm in this new environment. In this paper, we present an exact method for schedulability test of periodic tasksets in dual core environments. The result is less pessimistic than bound tests and the reason for the pessimism is twofold:
• Bound tests is sufficient but not necessary in multicore scheduling so far.
• In bound tests, the WCET of a task is fixed and it is equal WCET in cold cache for reliable.

The first reason results in bound tests rejecting some schedulable tasksets. For the second reason, in practice the WCET of a task is different in a cold cache and a warm cache, which is not used by bound tests until now. By our test, it is easy to determine whether a taskset is schedulable for preemptive RM algorithm under cache warm-up overheads. If the taskset is not schedulable, one should change scheduling algorithm or hardware architecture (e.g., [1]).

Our model now is limited to dual cores. We will expand to more cores by decreasing state space or changing model checker. Actually task migration not only brings cache warmup overheads but also introduces increasing traffic on the network-on-chip interconnect, which makes schedulability test difficulty. Although simulation-based schedulability test has some drawbacks, it can handle more cores. We will make comparison between simulation and our method. In addition, until now there is no continuous modeling method for schedulability test in multicore scheduling. We plan to make more exact schedulability analyses in multicore environments.
